title: I don't know how to pray
seoTitle: How to Pray When You Don't Know What to Say
description: Don't know how to pray? A simple daily pattern, the Lord's Prayer as an outline, praying the Psalms, and honest help for when God seems silent.
summary: Where to start, what to say, what to do when your mind wanders, and how to keep praying when heaven seems quiet.
askedAs: what to say when you pray
how to pray when you can't
what does the Bible say about prayer
answer: You want to pray, or you feel you ought to, and when you try, the words won't come, or they come out stiff and secondhand, like a speech to the ceiling. Maybe no one ever taught you, or you prayed once and it has gone quiet, or you aren't sure anyone is listening. The first disciples stood where you are: they asked Jesus to teach them, and he gave them words. Start there. Pray [the Lord's Prayer](/study/bible/matthew/6) slowly, one line at a time, and after each line say in your own plain words what it means for you today. Then tell God one true thing you're carrying. That is a real prayer, and it's enough for tonight.
happening:
When you say *I don't know how to pray*, you're usually not asking for a technique. You're describing what happens when you try. You close your eyes, and within a minute you're reciting phrases you picked up somewhere, or planning tomorrow's errands. You feel self-conscious, as if you're performing for someone who may or may not be in the room. You hear someone pray aloud with ease and assume they learned a secret you missed. Or you used to pray, and it shrank to meals and emergencies, and the silence has gone on so long that starting again feels like calling someone you've neglected for years. Some who read this aren't sure anyone is there at all, and they're curious anyway.

The usual explanations each hold some truth. The spiritual one says you'd pray more if you loved God more, and there's something to it, because attention follows love. But guilt is a poor teacher, and it turns prayer into a test you keep failing when it's really a language you haven't learned yet. The practical one says prayer is a habit, and screens have trained our attention to jump from one thing to the next. That's true too, yet you can build a flawless habit and still feel no one is on the other end. The skeptic's explanation says prayer is talking to yourself, and whatever calm it brings, you'd get by saying your worries aloud in an empty room. As far as it goes, that's fair: naming a fear plainly does steady a person. But Christian prayer has never claimed to be a calming technique. It claims to be an answer to someone who spoke first.

What all three leave out is that nobody starts out knowing how. Prayer is learned, like any language, and the men who lived with Jesus had to ask.

Sometimes prayer fades along with everything else: sleep, appetite, joy, interest in the people you love. When that's so, the silence is about more than prayer, and it's worth talking with a doctor or counselor as well as a pastor. Needing that help is no mark against your faith, and a weight like that isn't meant to be carried alone.

scripture.intro: The Bible is short on method and long on examples of people learning to pray, clumsily and honestly: disciples asking to be taught, a man knocking at midnight, David telling God he feels forgotten, Jesus asking for what he didn't receive, and an apostle admitting that none of us knows how. Read slowly, and notice who is speaking to whom.

passages.text: One day in a place where Jesus had just finished praying, one of His disciples requested, “Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples.” So Jesus told them, “When you pray, say: ‘Father, hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come. Give us each day our daily bread. And forgive us our sins, for we also forgive everyone who sins against us. And lead us not into temptation.’”
passages.reading: Luke shows Jesus praying at the turning points of his ministry, and here one of his disciples speaks up the moment he finishes. They had grown up among a praying people, and still, after watching him, they asked to be taught like beginners. Jesus didn't scold them, and his answer was words rather than a method: “When you pray, say” (verse 2). The prayer opens with “Father,” a family word, not a courtier's. It asks for God's name to be honored and his kingdom to come before it asks anything for us, and then it asks for ordinary things: bread for today, forgiveness, help against temptation. If you don't know what to pray, you may pray this word for word and mean as much of it as you can. He told them to.

passages.text: So I tell you: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; he who seeks finds; and to him who knocks, the door will be opened. What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will give him a snake instead? Or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? So if you who are evil know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!
passages.reading: Just before this, Jesus tells of a man who wakes a friend at midnight to borrow bread for a guest. The friend grumbles from bed, then gets up anyway, “because of the man’s persistence” (verse 8). The argument runs from lesser to greater: if a grumpy friend will get up, and if fathers Jesus calls evil still won't hand a hungry son a snake, how much more will your Father give. Then notice what he promises: “the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him” (verse 13), God's own presence, rather than everything on your list. Your requests still matter; he has just told you to ask for bread. But what Jesus promises here, to everyone who asks, is God himself. If *father* is a hard word for you because of the father you had, or never had, watch how Jesus argues. He doesn't measure God by your father. He measures every father by God, and all of us fall short.

passages.text: How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever? How long will You hide Your face from me? How long must I wrestle in my soul, with sorrow in my heart each day? How long will my enemy dominate me? Consider me and respond, O LORD my God. Give light to my eyes, lest I sleep in death, lest my enemy say, “I have overcome him,” and my foes rejoice when I fall. But I have trusted in Your loving devotion; my heart will rejoice in Your salvation. I will sing to the LORD, for He has been good to me.
passages.reading: The heading credits this psalm to David and hands it to the choirmaster, so Israel sang it in worship, complaint and all. It asks “how long” four times in two verses. When prayer feels like talking to the ceiling, this psalm gives you permission, and words, to say so to God's face, and saying so is prayer, because it's said to him. Another psalm makes the invitation plain: “pour out your hearts before Him” (Psalm 62:8). Nothing in David's circumstances changes by the end, but he finds his footing again: “But I have trusted in Your loving devotion” (verse 5). That turn is no formula for ending every prayer on a bright note, since Psalm 88 never turns at all, but it shows what honest speech to a faithful God can do to the one who speaks.

passages.text: Going a little farther, He fell to the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour would pass from Him. “Abba, Father,” He said, “all things are possible for You. Take this cup from Me. Yet not what I will, but what You will.”
passages.reading: It's the night before the cross, and at Gethsemane Jesus has told his closest friends that his sorrow is crushing him. He calls God “Abba,” the Aramaic word a son used for his father, and asks for exactly what he wants: take this away. He doesn't dress it up or pretend to want the cross. Then comes the sentence that turns a plea into surrender: “Yet not what I will, but what You will” (verse 36). The cup wasn't taken. Yet Hebrews, remembering prayers like this, says he “was heard because of His reverence” (Hebrews 5:7), and on the third day the Father raised him from the dead. His friends, meanwhile, fell asleep, and Jesus said, “the spirit is willing, but the body is weak” (Mark 14:38). If you've asked and not received, or dozed off trying to pray, you're in company Jesus kept.

passages.text: In the same way, the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know how we ought to pray, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words. And He who searches our hearts knows the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God.
passages.reading: Paul filled his letters with prayers for his churches, and still he writes, “we do not know how we ought to pray” (verse 26). He includes himself. The chapter around these verses is full of groaning: the whole creation groans like a woman in labor (verse 22), we groan as we wait for our bodies to be made new (verse 23), and here the Spirit intercedes for us with groans of his own. Paul is writing to believers, and this is his promise to them: when all you can manage is a sigh, a name, or tears, the Spirit is praying in you, and the Father who searches hearts understands exactly what's being asked. Nothing in that sigh is lost on him.

whyHard:
If prayer is a language, why do so many of us feel we should already be fluent? Part of the answer is a picture of prayer that most Christians in history would have found strange: real prayer comes straight from the heart, in fresh words of your own, and anything borrowed or repeated is second-rate.

For most of the church's life, people learned to pray the way Israel did, by praying words they'd been given. The Psalms put a hundred and fifty songs and prayers in the mouths of God's people. One of the oldest Christian writings outside the New Testament, the Didache, sets down the Lord's Prayer and tells believers to pray it three times a day. No one expected a new Christian to invent prayer, any more than we expect a toddler to invent English.

The suspicion of given words has better reasons behind it than we sometimes admit. Jesus warned against praying like those who “think that by their many words they will be heard” (Matthew 6:7), and anyone who has recited a prayer while planning lunch knows the danger. Many free-church Christians have long preferred prayer from the heart to prayer read from a page, and for a sound reason: God wants the person praying, and a recitation can hide the person. But somewhere along the way many of us let the heart become the source of prayer rather than the place prayer is meant to reach. Then a culture that equates sincerity with spontaneity finished the job, and we told people with empty hearts and no words that they would have to produce both.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer saw the mistake. In 1940, in a short book on the Psalms, he warned that Christians go badly wrong when they think the heart can pray by itself. The heart can wish and hope and sigh, he argued, but we learn to pray the way a child learns to speak, by repeating the words the Father speaks first. That's why he called the Psalms the prayer book of the Bible. They hold some of the most honest words in Scripture, and they're God's words, handed back to us to pray.

A second difficulty weighs most on the skeptic, though believers feel it too. The philosopher Charles Taylor has described how the modern West moved from a world where it was nearly impossible not to believe in God to one where faith, even for the devout, is one option among others. We pray inside that world. The default sense of the room is that it's empty, and many thoughtful people are sure it is. I came to faith from atheism, so I won't call that sense foolish. But it tells you about the age you live in, and it can't tell you who is in the room.

The third difficulty is one pastors like me have to own. We've often taught prayer as a way of getting things, so when the things don't come, people conclude that they prayed wrong or that no one heard. And a long, polished prayer from the front of a church can teach a whole room that prayer is a performance for the gifted.

Put those together and you get a person who thinks prayer should come naturally, half suspects no one is listening, and judges it by results. Of course that person doesn't know how to pray; nobody does by nature. You were never meant to know how. You were meant to ask.

thisWeek.intro: You don't need a new life to start praying, only a few minutes, a place, and some words to borrow. Choose one or two of these this week. A small habit you keep will teach you more than a big one you drop by Thursday.

steps.title: Pick a time and a place
steps.body: Choose one time you can keep every day, before you look at your phone in the morning or just before sleep, and one place: a chair, the car, the edge of your bed. Give it five minutes, in this order if it helps: the Lord's Prayer, a few lines of a psalm, one or two names, and one true sentence about your day. Praying at a set time is older than the church: “In the morning, O LORD, You hear my voice” (Psalm 5:3). If you miss a day, skip the lecture to yourself and come back.

steps.title: Use the Lord's Prayer as an outline
steps.body: In 1535, when his barber asked him how to pray, Martin Luther wrote him a little book teaching him to pray the Lord's Prayer one line at a time, in his own words. Try it with [Matthew 6:9-13](/study/bible/matthew/6). At “hallowed be Your name,” thank God for something true of him. At “Your kingdom come,” name a place you long to see his way win. At “daily bread,” ask plainly for what today needs. At “forgive us our debts,” name a wrong you've done and a person you need to forgive. At “lead us not into temptation,” name the temptation you can see coming. If a line leaves you wordless, say it and move on.

steps.title: Pray a psalm, slowly
steps.body: The Psalms are the oldest prayer book the church has, meant to be prayed as well as read; Jesus prayed the opening line of Psalm 22 from the cross (Mark 15:34). Pick one: Psalm 23 when you need to trust, Psalm 13 when God feels far away, Psalm 51 when you've done wrong, Psalm 103 when you want to give thanks. Read it slowly, aloud if you can. When a line is true for you, say it to God in your own words. When it isn't true for you today, pray it for someone it fits. In time, borrowed words become your own.

steps.title: Pray for people by name
steps.body: Write three to five names on a card and keep it where you pray. Say each name to God and ask for one specific thing. Jesus prayed this way; the night before he died he told Peter, “I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith will not fail” (Luke 22:32). Ask a friend what they'd like you to pray for, and a week later ask how it's going. Don't promise anyone an outcome. Promise to keep bringing them to God, and keep the promise.

steps.title: When your mind wanders
steps.body: It will, usually within a minute. Brother Lawrence, a lay brother who cooked for years in a monastery kitchen in seventeenth-century Paris, gave plain counsel about this in a letter later gathered into *The Practice of the Presence of God*: don't fret when your mind wanders, because fretting scatters it further; bring it back quietly, as often as it takes. Praying aloud in a low voice, writing your prayers down, or walking can help. Keep a scrap of paper nearby for the errands that surface. When someone's face comes to mind, take it as an assignment and pray for them.

steps.title: When it feels like talking to the ceiling
steps.body: Keep the appointment anyway, and tell God the truth about it. *It feels like I'm talking to the ceiling* is itself a prayer; Psalm 13 is built from sentences like it. Don't grade your prayer by how it felt. When you can't pray alone, pray with others: find a church that prays aloud together, or ask a friend to pray with you by phone once a week. Anyone who prays for long meets stretches like this, and coming back is the practice.

moreHelp.body:
Trouble praying is usually a spiritual matter, and a pastor or a friend who prays is the right first call. Sometimes, though, the silence in prayer is part of something wider. If you've lost interest in nearly everything, not only prayer, if your sleep or appetite has changed, if you feel hopeless or worthless, and it has lasted weeks, see a doctor or a licensed counselor. Do the same if prayer has become a place of fear: if you feel you must repeat prayers or confessions perfectly or something terrible will happen, or you never feel forgiven however often you confess. Needing that help is no sign that God is angry with you. And if anyone uses prayer to control you, insisting God told them what you must do, that is spiritual abuse. Talk with someone you trust outside that relationship, and if it's someone at home and you're afraid, contact the National Domestic Violence Hotline.

To find a counselor, ask your doctor for a referral, check your insurer's directory, or ask a pastor which counselors nearby they trust. If you want a Christian counselor, make sure they're licensed in your state; your state's licensing board can confirm it.
signs: You have thoughts of ending your life or of not wanting to be alive. Call or text 988 now, or 911 if you are in danger.
Prayer has gone quiet along with your sleep, appetite, or interest in the people you love, for two weeks or more.
Fear of praying wrong, or of never being forgiven, is taking hours of your day.
Someone uses prayer, or claims about what God told them, to control or frighten you.
moreHelp.firstCall: You don't need the right words. You might say, *I can't pray anymore, and it's not only prayer. I'm not sleeping, and I've lost interest in most things.* Say how long it has been. If your faith matters to you, say so: *I'm a Christian, and I'd like a counselor who respects that.* To a pastor, it can be as simple as *I don't know how to pray, and I'd like someone to pray with me for a few weeks.*
moreHelp.cost: Talking with a pastor costs nothing. Counseling fees vary, so ask about sliding-scale fees, look for a community mental health center or a university training clinic, and check whether your employer offers an employee assistance program, which often covers a few free sessions. Some churches keep a benevolence fund to help with counseling costs, and it's fine to ask.

helping.body: Maybe your child asked how to pray, or your husband or wife has quietly stopped, or someone in your group goes silent whenever it's time to pray aloud. The most useful thing you can do is pray with them, briefly and plainly, so they hear that ordinary words are allowed. Don't use the prayer to make a point; people notice. Offer words to borrow: the Lord's Prayer, a psalm, a written prayer. With a child, a sentence or two at bedtime in her own words is a whole prayer. If a friend doesn't believe but is curious, don't press; tell them honest prayer can begin with an *if*. If you lead a group or a church, pray in public the way you hope people will pray at home, plainly. And when someone tells you their prayers went unanswered, resist the urge to explain. Sit with them, grieve the no together, and don't pretend to know why it came.
say: Nobody starts out knowing how. Even the disciples had to ask.
Want to pray together? I'll keep it short.
You can borrow words. The Lord's Prayer is a good start.
You can tell God you feel nothing, or that you're angry.
What would you like me to pray for this week?
dontSay: God always answers if you ask the right way.
There must be sin blocking your prayers.
Prayer is easy. Just talk to him.
helping.next: Pray with them once this week and send them one psalm. If they want more, invite them to work through [Prayer: A Bible Study on Learning to Pray](/studyguides/prayer) with you or a small group. Check in again in a week or two. If you notice the signs above, help them make the call to a doctor or counselor, and offer to sit with them while they do.

prayer:
Father, I don't know how to do this. I'm not sure I ever did. Some days I'm not sure you're there, and I'm telling you because you already know.

The disciples asked Jesus to teach them, so I'm asking too. Teach me to pray. Give me words when I have none, and when I can't find even one, let your Spirit carry what I can't say. You know what I need before I ask. I'll ask anyway, because your Son told me to.

Here are the names I carry. Here is the thing I've asked for so long that I've stopped expecting an answer. If your answer is no, don't let me mistake your no for your absence. Jesus asked you to take the cup away, and you didn't, and on the third day you raised him from the dead.

When my mind wanders, bring it back. When all I have is complaint, receive it, as you received David's. Keep me knocking, morning and evening, at the door your Son said would open.

Our Father, hallowed be your name. Amen.

faq.q: What should I say when I pray?
faq.a: Start with the truth: tell God what's actually going on, in plain words, the way you'd talk to someone who knows everything about you and stayed anyway. If you want a pattern, many Christians use four movements: praise God for who he is, confess where you've gone wrong, thank him for specific things, and ask for what you and others need. Or pray the Lord's Prayer a line at a time. One sentence you mean is a whole prayer.

The Bible's answer is yes, and more: he knows what you'll say before you say it. “Even before a word is on my tongue, You know all about it, O LORD” (Psalm 139:4). Jesus told his disciples that the Father knows what they need before they ask (Matthew 6:8), so you don't have to impress him or wear him down. Being heard isn't the same as receiving what you asked for, and Scripture is honest about that. If you feel unheard, tell him so. Psalm 13 begins there.

faq.q: Why doesn't God answer my prayers?
faq.a: Sometimes God doesn't give what we ask, and the Bible doesn't hide it. Paul pleaded three times to be rid of what he called a thorn in his flesh, and the answer was, “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Jesus asked in Gethsemane for the cup to pass, and it didn't. Promises like “whatever you ask in My name” (John 14:13) aren't blank checks; Jesus's own prayer shows what asking in his name looks like: “not what I will, but what You will” (Mark 14:36). What God does promise is his Spirit (Luke 11:13). So keep asking, and tell him honestly what the silence is like.

faq.q: Can I pray if I'm not sure God exists?
faq.a: Yes, and you can be honest about it. You don't have to pretend to a faith you don't have; you can say, *God, if you're there, I want to know.* The Bible is full of people praying from inside their doubt. A desperate father told Jesus, “I do believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24), and Jesus helped him. No one can promise you a feeling or a sign on your schedule. But reading a Gospel and praying honestly as you go is a fair way to find out whether anyone is listening.

faq.q: What do I do when I can't pray at all?
faq.a: Some days the words are simply gone. Let one word be your prayer: *help*, or someone's name, or *Jesus*. Paul says that when we don't know how to pray, “the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words” (Romans 8:26). Tell a friend or your pastor that you can't pray right now, and ask them to pray for you. And if the silence has come with a heaviness that won't lift, talk with a doctor or counselor too.

slots.note: James could say, in his own words, how prayer looked to him as an atheist and what his first prayers were like after he came to faith. The paragraph on the sense of an empty room is written to stand without it.

In the Luke 11:9-13 reading, James could add what the word Father meant to a boy raised without one, and what being a father of five sons has taught him about Jesus's how-much-more argument. The reading stands without it.
James could describe the daily prayer habit he actually keeps as a pastor, as one real example beside the six steps.
James could add, in his own words, how he has taught his sons to pray.

reviewed.notes: Writer's check. validate-needs.mjs clean (word ranges, Scripture verbatim BSB per reference, double quotes reserved for Scripture, forbidden language, no em-dash, no exclamation outside Scripture, no phone numbers, every link live and not redirected). Every Scripture quotation copied from scripts/bsb.mjs; Psalm 13 is quoted without its superscription. Kit links resolved against the route table and manifests; /writing/psalms-as-prayer-not-poetry (vercel redirect) and /prayer-in-the-dark (client redirect to /books) deliberately left out; essay labels use the retitled /writing titles in content-data.json. No statistics and no quotations except Scripture. Named witnesses (the Didache, Bonhoeffer 1940, Charles Taylor, Luther 1535, Brother Lawrence) are paraphrased and listed in sources; each was confirmed through search-engine excerpts of the cited pages because direct page fetches were blocked, so re-open each source before publishing. The contested reading of anaideia in Luke 11:8 was avoided; the page follows the BSB's persistence. James's first person is limited to stance (a Baptist pastor, came to faith from atheism, pastors like me); four slots left for his own story. Read as the midnight reader (one clear step on the first screen), the skeptic (his explanation conceded, unanswered prayer and the in-My-name promises handled honestly), and the pastor (pastors implicated, public prayer addressed). Care: 988 and 911 in the signs, spiritual abuse named, no diagnosis. Length is a little above the brief's aim of about 4,000; every section is inside its spec range.
